title: Preface
summary: Exxon Mobil Corporation’s 2021 Form 10-K is its annual report for the year ended December 31, 2021. It identifies the company’s incorporation, tax ID, headquarters, contact number, and registered common stock and notes listed on the New York Stock Exchange. The filing states its reporting and filer status, compliance with filing, interactive-data, and internal-control requirements, and that it is not a shell company or emerging growth company. It reports nonaffiliate voting-stock market value above $267 billion and 4,233,592,429 common shares outstanding as of January 31, 2022; the 2022 proxy statement is incorporated by reference for Part III.

title: EXXON MOBIL CORPORATION FORM 10-K FOR THE FISCAL YEAR ENDED DECEMBER 31, 2021
summary: Exxon Mobil Corporation’s 2021 Form 10-K table of contents lists Parts I–IV: business, risks, staff comments, properties, legal and mine-safety matters, and executive officers; stock and shareholder matters, management’s analysis, market risk, financial statements, accounting matters, controls, and other disclosures; governance, compensation, ownership, related-party transactions, and auditor fees; and exhibits, financial schedules, the 10-K summary, exhibit index, signatures, and certifications.

title: PART I

nodes.title: ITEM 1. BUSINESS
nodes.summary: ExxonMobil’s history, global operations, core oil, gas, petrochemical and lower-emission businesses, affiliates, competition, and locations of segment and reserve disclosures are described. The text covers research, patents and licensing; long-term employee development, compensation, workforce diversity, community investment and employee counts; regulatory and environmental obligations, expenditures and forecasts; references for other operational risks; and the company website’s SEC filings, governance materials, and the SEC’s filing database.

nodes.title: ITEM 1A. RISK FACTORS
Supply and Demand
nodes.summary: ExxonMobil’s results and financial condition face risks from volatile commodity prices and margins, shaped by supply and demand. Demand risks include recessions, geopolitical, regulatory, trade, public-health and financial-market disruptions; COVID-19 impacts; and shifts in efficiency, weather, alternative energy, technology, consumer preferences and incomes. Supply risks include new sources and capacity, recovery technologies, OPEC/OPEC+ quotas, emissions policies, conflict, disasters and operational or logistics disruptions. Interest rates, inflation, currency movements and local market conditions can also affect results and hedging or trading instruments.

nodes.title: Government and Political Factors
nodes.summary: ExxonMobil’s performance may be harmed by political and regulatory developments, including restricted access to oil and gas resources, foreign-investment limits, trade restrictions, and sanctions that constrain operations or advantage competitors. Weak legal systems can create unpredictable government actions and hinder contract enforcement. Legal, regulatory, and policy changes may raise taxes or compliance costs, impose price or efficiency controls, delay permits, restrict operations, mandate disclosures, or cancel contracts and expropriate assets. Litigation and enforcement may bring costly or unpredictable outcomes. Civil unrest, sabotage, terrorism, cyberattacks, and national-security measures may increase security costs or interrupt operations.

nodes.title: Climate Change and the Energy Transition
nodes.summary: The text outlines risks and uncertainties in the energy transition: net-zero ambitions and scenarios depend on uncertain technologies, policies, markets, and timely investment decisions. Emissions restrictions—including carbon pricing, mandates, permitting limits, and pressure on financing—could raise costs, delay projects, weaken hydrocarbon competitiveness and demand, and shift demand to lower-carbon alternatives. ExxonMobil’s Low Carbon Solutions business pursues CCS, hydrogen, biofuels, efficiency, and other technologies through research and partnerships, but success depends on cost-competitive innovation and supportive policies and markets. Delayed support or restrictions on supply without matching demand reductions could cause price volatility, inflation, energy shortages, and economic or policy disruption.

nodes.title: Operational and Other Factors
nodes.summary: ExxonMobil’s results depend on managing controllable operational factors and, for non-operated projects, co-venturers. Key risks include exploration and development success; effective major-project and portfolio management, including negotiations, costs, schedules, divestments, and retained liabilities; operational efficiency and talent; research, development, and adapting to technology and policy changes; safety, environmental, business controls, and enterprise risk management; cybersecurity threats and third-party disruptions; preparedness for severe weather and other emergencies; limited insurance availability and affordability; intense competition from private and state-owned firms and alternative energy; and reputational harm. These factors may affect performance and make forward-looking plans and projections differ materially from actual outcomes.

The section describes risks to ExxonMobil’s results and financial condition from volatile supply, demand, prices, margins, economic and market conditions; political, legal, regulatory, security, and geopolitical developments; climate policies and uncertainties in the energy transition; and operational, project, technology, safety, environmental, cybersecurity, emergency, insurance, competitive, and reputational factors. It also notes uncertainties affecting low-carbon investments and the possibility that actual outcomes may differ materially from plans and projections.

title: ITEM 2. PROPERTIES

nodes.title: ITEM 2. PROPERTIES (intro)
nodes.summary: Reports ExxonMobil’s year-end 2021 proved oil and gas reserves by product, geography, development status, and consolidated subsidiaries versus equity companies, using specified gas-to-oil conversion and average monthly first-day prices. Higher prices brought some quantities into proved reserves; no subsequent major event significantly changed estimates. It discusses production variability and reserve-estimation uncertainties, the geological, engineering, seismic, and software methods supporting 2021 additions, and the experienced, independent reserves group’s oversight, database controls, review, approval, and management endorsement procedures.

nodes.title: 2. Proved Undeveloped Reserves
nodes.summary: At year-end 2021, ExxonMobil reported 6.3 billion oil-equivalent barrels of proved undeveloped reserves (34% of total proved reserves), up from 5.0 billion in 2020. Development transferred 0.5 billion barrels to developed reserves, while discoveries and extensions added 1.3 billion and revisions added 0.6 billion. The company invested $8.0 billion to advance these reserves, 65% of Upstream capital and exploration spending. Long project lead times and infrastructure constraints leave some reserves undeveloped for five or more years, mainly in Australia, Canada, Kazakhstan, the United States, and the UAE. ExxonMobil expects production, though timing and recovery depend on project progress, reservoir, regulatory, funding, investment, policy, market, and price factors. The text describes the relevant projects in Australia (Gorgon Jansz compression), Canada (Cold Lake), Kazakhstan (Tengiz-Korolev development), and the UAE (Upper Zakum development and drilling).

title: D. Summary of Acreage Terms

nodes.title: Oil and Gas Acreage Terms by Country
nodes.summary: Summarizes how oil and gas exploration and production rights are acquired and how long they last. In the United States, rights are generally leased from government or private mineral owners, with exploration terms of 1–10 years and production continuing while production lasts; certain leases can extend beyond exploration, and private mineral interests may be acquired outright. Canada describes onshore renewals tied to work and production, offshore exploration terms and work commitments, 25-year production licenses, and indefinite significant-discovery licenses. Argentina outlines concession terms, extensions, offshore exploration licenses, and older provincial concessions. Brazil distinguishes concession and production-sharing exploration and production periods. Guyana describes licenses and agreements with exploration periods up to 10 years and production terms of 20 years, extendable by 10.

nodes.title: EUROPE
nodes.summary: Germany grants exploration concessions for up to five years, extendable repeatedly for up to three years with minimum work commitments; production licenses usually last 20–25 years and may be extended while production continues. In the Netherlands, licenses issued since 2003 have terms defined by the license according to required activities. Earlier production rights retain existing terms: onshore licenses were indefinite before 1988, then typically 35–45 years; offshore licenses were 40 years before 1976, then typically 15–40 years. UK terms vary by licensing round: early licenses commonly had six-year initial terms, area relinquishment, and possible 40-year extensions, with distinct rules for producing, development, and other areas. Most current traditional licenses provide four-year exploration terms, a possible four-year extension, and an 18-year production term, requiring acreage relinquishment at specified stages.

nodes.title: AFRICA
nodes.summary: The text outlines African oil and gas licensing and contract terms. Angola uses negotiated contracts with 3–4-year exploration periods, extensions, and 20–30-year production terms. Chad permits last five years, renewable twice, with 30-year production extended to 2050. Equatorial Guinea uses state-negotiated production-sharing contracts and 30-year crude production terms. Mozambique concession contracts and Area 4 and other block EPCCs specify exploration expiries and 30-year development/production periods. Nigeria’s deepwater PSCs, OPLs and OMLs cover exploration, conversion after commercial discovery, relinquishment, renewals, and NNPC joint ventures; rules differ for pre-1969 and later OMLs, including their durations, tax terms and relinquishment requirements.

nodes.title: FORWARD-LOOKING STATEMENTS
nodes.summary: The section identifies projections, goals, strategies, emission roadmaps, and energy-demand scenarios as forward-looking statements, whose actual outcomes may differ materially. It lists potential outcomes and risks, including market, economic, policy, pandemic, geopolitical, regulatory, operational, technological, financing, project, and litigation factors. Energy models and scenarios rely on uncertain assumptions; references to third-party or net-zero scenarios are not endorsements or predictions. ExxonMobil makes investment decisions through its own planning process, while sometimes testing resilience against alternative assumptions.

nodes.title: OVERVIEW
OVERVIEW (intro)
nodes.summary: Management is responsible for ExxonMobil’s financial analysis and statements, which reflect its integrated oil, gas, products, chemicals, specialty-products, and lower-emission businesses. Its segments were Upstream, Downstream, and Chemical, with voluntary regional disclosures. From April 2022, Chemical and Downstream were combined into Product Solutions, alongside Upstream and Low Carbon Solutions; shared technology and services support these businesses. ExxonMobil cites its resources, finances, technology, disciplined investments, and integrated model as strengths that help manage commodity-price risk. Annual corporate planning uses the Energy Outlook, field-production profiles, and regional assumptions for prices, margins, volumes, costs, emissions prices, and exchange rates to guide investment evaluation. Major investments are assessed under varied market conditions and later reviewed for lessons and improvements.

nodes.title: BUSINESS ENVIRONMENT Long-Term Business Outlook
nodes.summary: ExxonMobil’s Energy Outlook guides long-term planning and investment, projecting global energy supply and demand through 2050 using current trends, multiple scenarios—including IPCC lower-2°C and IEA net-zero—and indicators for adapting projections. It anticipates population and economic growth driving energy demand up nearly 15%, despite efficiency gains, with developing countries leading growth. Electricity demand rises about 75%; renewables, gas and nuclear expand as coal declines. Transport energy and liquid-fuels demand grow, though light-vehicle fuel use falls; diverse oil sources and timely investment remain important. Natural gas grows strongly, supported by unconventional supply and LNG. Oil remains the largest energy source, while gas gains share and renewables and nuclear expand. Technology and substantial investment will support supply. The Outlook incorporates evolving climate policies, Paris Agreement NDCs, sector-specific measures and assumed OECD carbon costs, while monitoring newer commitments; projections rely on internal analysis and public information.

nodes.title: Leading the Drive to Net Zero
nodes.summary: The company aims to lead the energy transition while meeting demand for essential products, targeting net-zero Scope 1 and 2 emissions from operated assets by 2050. It is developing facility-specific, regularly updated reduction roadmaps for assets covering about 90% of emissions by year-end 2022 and the rest in 2023, identifying opportunities, investment needs, and policy requirements. By 2030 versus 2016, plans target 20–30% lower corporate-wide emissions intensity and about 20% lower absolute emissions, with specific upstream, methane, and flaring intensity and emissions reductions. The company established Low Carbon Solutions in 2021 to develop carbon capture and storage, hydrogen, and biofuels, investing in lower-emission technologies and using research, emerging technology assessment, and global collaboration to expand opportunities. Stronger policy could accelerate deployment and create further investment opportunities; the new business will initially be reported under Corporate and Financing. Strategy draws on scale, integration, technology, and people to build competitive, resilient businesses.

nodes.title: Recent Business Environment
nodes.summary: The text describes the 2020 COVID-19 demand collapse and rising production that increased inventories and sharply lowered energy prices, followed by an uneven recovery through 2021; oil and gas prices and chemical margins strengthened, while downstream margins and jet demand lagged. It discusses pandemic-related inflation, supply-chain and labor constraints, cost pressures, nearly $5 billion in structural savings since 2019 (including about $2 billion annually from workforce reductions), and further streamlining. ExxonMobil’s Upstream strategy prioritizes selective, low-cost growth, technology, efficiency, emissions reduction, and operational excellence; it outlines expected shifts toward Americas and unconventional, deepwater, and LNG production, projects in Guyana, Brazil, the Permian, Mozambique, Papua New Guinea, and Golden Pass, factors affecting volumes, long-term supply-and-demand price drivers, and scenario testing to manage price risk.

nodes.title: Key Recent Events
nodes.summary: The text reviews 2021 progress in key developments: Guyana’s Stabroek discoveries, Liza Unity’s arrival and February 2022 production start, Payara’s planned 2024 start-up, and Yellowtail’s planned 2025 first oil; Permian output averaged about 460 koebd, rose nearly 100 koebd year over year, exceeded expectations, and improved drilling and capital efficiency, alongside a 2030 Scope 1 and 2 net-zero goal; Brazil’s Bacalhau Phase 1 reached final investment decision, targeting 2024 start-up; and Mozambique’s Coral South FLNG remained on plan for 2022 start-up, with Coral Sul beginning its tow. The excerpt then introduces upstream financial results, organized by U.S., non-U.S., and total earnings, identified items, and earnings excluding identified items.

nodes.title: 2021 Upstream Earnings Factor Analysis
nodes.summary: The text presents 2021 and 2020 upstream earnings factor analyses. In 2021, higher realizations increased earnings by $14.96 billion, unfavorable volume and mix reduced them by $340 million, and other factors added $2.04 billion, mainly from $1.36 billion in lower expenses and favorable one-time tax items. Identified-item losses were $543 million in 2021, reflecting impairments and contractual provisions partly offset by a U.K. North Sea divestment gain, versus a $19.694 billion 2020 loss, mainly dry-gas impairments. In 2020, lower realizations reduced earnings by $11.21 billion, volume and mix by $300 million, while other factors added $1.17 billion, mainly lower expenses. Identified items shifted from a $4.434 billion 2019 gain, primarily Norway divestment, to the 2020 loss. A footnote directs readers to definitions of identified items and earnings excluding them.

nodes.title: Upstream Operational Results
nodes.summary: Reports upstream production for 2019–2021 by region for crude oil, natural gas liquids, bitumen and synthetic oil; natural gas available for sale; and oil-equivalent production, using a conversion of six million cubic feet of gas per thousand barrels. In 2021, liquids output fell 60 thousand barrels per day from 2020 as entitlements, decline and divestments outweighed higher demand and growth; gas rose 66 million cubic feet daily, with demand gains partly offset by divestments and Groningen limits. In 2020, liquids fell 37 thousand barrels daily due to mandates, divestments and weaker demand, partly offset by growth and less downtime; gas fell 923 million cubic feet daily, with divestments, lower demand and more downtime partly offset by growth.

It then describes ExxonMobil Downstream’s global, integrated business and strategy, 2021 refining-margin and fuel-demand recovery, near-term outlook and restarted projects, factors driving margins and volatility, integration and growth in fuels and lubricants, climate-policy risks, and portfolio decisions focused on resilience and profitability.

nodes.title: Key Recent Events
nodes.summary: ExxonMobil planned over 40,000 barrels per day of lower-emission fuels by 2025, including a renewable diesel unit at Strathcona and supply agreements with Global Clean Energy and Biojet AS. It converted refineries in Slagen and Altona into import terminals, while Refining New Zealand planned a similar conversion for 2022; ExxonMobil holds a 17% minority stake there. The excerpt also introduces downstream financial results, with U.S., non-U.S., and total earnings, identified items, and earnings excluding identified items.

nodes.title: 2021 Downstream Earnings Factor Analysis
nodes.summary: The text presents 2021 and 2020 downstream earnings factor analyses, with earnings figures in millions of dollars. In 2021, earnings rose by $1.92 billion from improved refining conditions, $100 million from demand recovery and favorable mix, and $300 million from lower expenses, partly offset by unfavorable foreign exchange and LIFO effects. In 2020, margins reduced earnings by $3.82 billion amid weaker refining conditions; volume added $370 million as yield improvements partly offset weaker demand; and other factors added $900 million, with expense savings partly offset by LIFO impacts. The 2020 identified-items loss was $859 million, mainly from impairments and unfavorable tax items. A note refers readers to the glossary for definitions of identified items and earnings excluding them.

nodes.title: Downstream Operational Results
nodes.summary: The table reports 2019–2021 refinery throughput and petroleum product sales by region and product category, in thousands of barrels daily; sales are net of purchases and sales contracts with the same counterparty. The Chemical section describes ExxonMobil’s global petrochemical business, its technology, scale, integration, operational reliability, investment advantages, and cost discipline. Despite COVID-19 impacts, resilient demand in key segments and supply disruptions improved industry margins in 2021, producing record earnings through optimization, logistics, and cost savings. Chemical demand is expected to outpace economic growth. The company completed an under-budget, ahead-of-schedule Corpus Christi joint-venture ethane cracker in late 2021 and restarted Gulf Coast growth projects in Baytown and Baton Rouge.

nodes.title: Key Recent Events
nodes.summary: ExxonMobil approved a multi-billion-dollar chemical complex in Huizhou, China, to serve expected demand for performance chemicals. It advanced a large plastic-waste recycling facility in Baytown, planned up to 500,000 metric tons of added annual capacity across sites by 2026, and began selling certified circular polymers in 2021. It acquired advanced-materials developer Materia for technologies with applications including wind turbines, electric vehicles, construction, and coatings, and sold its global Santoprene business, including U.S. and U.K. manufacturing sites, to Celanese.

nodes.title: Chemical Financial Results
nodes.summary: Chemical earnings are shown for 2019–2021 by U.S. and non-U.S. results, identified items, and earnings excluding identified items, in millions of dollars; a note directs readers to the terms definition. The 2021 factor analysis says stronger margins added $4,480 million, higher volumes added $250 million, and other factors added $360 million, mainly from favorable foreign exchange, lower expenses, and LIFO impacts. Identified items shifted from a $114 million loss in 2020, primarily impairments, to a $630 million gain in 2021 from the Santoprene divestment.

nodes.title: 2020 Chemical Earnings Factor Analysis
nodes.summary: 2020 chemical earnings factor analysis (in millions of dollars): stronger margins increased earnings by $930 million; lower volume decreased earnings by $150 million; other items increased earnings by $710 million, primarily due to lower expenses. Identified items were a $114 million loss, primarily from impairments. The footnote refers readers to Frequently Used Terms for definitions of identified items and earnings or loss excluding them.

nodes.title: Chemical Operational Results
nodes.summary: Chemical prime product sales (thousands of metric tons) were reported for 2021, 2020, and 2019, split between the United States, non-U.S., and worldwide: 9,724/16,608/26,332; 9,010/16,439/25,449; and 9,127/17,389/26,516, respectively. Data are net of purchases and sales contracts with the same counterparty. Corporate and Financing supports operating segments and Low Carbon Solutions, encompassing general administration, financing, and insurance; Low Carbon Solutions remains in this segment as it matures through technology commercialization and deployment.

nodes.title: Corporate and Financing Financial Results
nodes.summary: Corporate and Financing expenses fell to $2.636 billion in 2021 from $3.296 billion in 2020, mainly because prior-year severance and financing costs were lower; 2020 expenses had risen from 2019. Cash increased to $6.8 billion at year-end 2021, with operating, investing, and financing cash flows of $48.1 billion, $(10.2) billion, and $(35.4) billion; year-end 2020 cash was $4.4 billion. The report details annual cash sources and uses, operating, investing, and financing drivers, debt and equity changes, dividends, share repurchases, and liquidity, including credit lines and commercial paper. It discusses production decline and price-related cash-flow risks, project and investment variability, capital spending plans, portfolio diversification, asset divestitures and acquisitions, and concludes IBOR reform is not considered a material risk.

nodes.title: Contractual Obligations
nodes.summary: The text outlines ExxonMobil’s contractual obligations, including leases, debt, retirement and pension benefits, capital commitments, and purchase agreements; commodity commitments are offset by related sales, while take-or-pay and unconditional obligations totaled $30.031 billion, with $4.004 billion and $3.560 billion due in 2022 and 2023. It describes guarantees and pending litigation as unlikely to materially affect the company, reports unused credit lines and debt-to-capital ratios, and summarizes debt reduction from $67.6 billion in 2020 to $47.7 billion in 2021. It defines capital and exploration expenditures and presents 2021 and 2020 spending by business segment and geography.

nodes.title: Financial Strength, Contingencies and Capital Expenditures
nodes.summary: The page reports guarantees and management’s view that their potential effects are not material; unused credit lines, debt-to-capital ratios, and financial-strength strategy; 2020 liquidity measures and 2021 debt reduction; and management’s assessment that pending litigation is not expected to materially harm operations or financial condition. It also defines capital and exploration expenditures, explains their exclusions and management focus, and presents 2021 and 2020 expenditures by business segment and U.S./non-U.S. location.

The section outlines ExxonMobil’s integrated businesses, planning, investment and risk-management approach, long-term energy outlook, emissions goals and lower-carbon strategy, and recent market conditions and operating developments. It reviews Upstream, Downstream and Chemical strategies, projects, operations, production and sales, and financial results and earnings drivers, including identified items. It also covers Corporate and Financing results, cash flows, liquidity, debt, contractual obligations, guarantees, litigation, capital and exploration spending, and related risks.

nodes.title: CAPITAL AND EXPLORATION EXPENDITURES
nodes.summary: The Corporation reported contingent guarantees at year-end 2021, which management considers unlikely to materially affect its finances or operations. It had $10.7 billion in unused short-term and $0.6 billion in unused long-term committed credit lines, and described financial strength as a strategic advantage. After issuing $23.2 billion of debt and cutting costs in 2020, it reduced total debt from $67.6 billion to $47.7 billion in 2021 as prices and margins improved. Pending lawsuits are not expected to have a material adverse effect. The text defines Capex, presents 2019–2021 expenditure figures by business and region, and reports 2021 Capex of $16.6 billion, planned 2022 spending of $21–24 billion, and future firm commitments. It outlines upstream, downstream, and chemical spending trends, projects, and reserve development timing.

nodes.title: TAXES
nodes.summary: In 2021, ExxonMobil reported $40.6 billion in total income-statement taxes, up $17.8 billion from 2020: income tax expense was $7.6 billion versus a $5.6 billion benefit, the effective rate rose to 31% from 17% mainly due to jurisdictional earnings mix, and other taxes and duties increased to $33.0 billion. In 2020, total taxes fell to $22.8 billion from $38.5 billion in 2019; a $5.6 billion income-tax benefit, driven by asset impairments, replaced a $5.3 billion expense, and the effective rate declined to 17% from 34%, while other taxes fell to $28.4 billion. Environmental expenditures were $4.6 billion in 2021 ($1.2 billion capital, $3.4 billion other), compared with $4.5 billion in 2020; they cover prevention and remediation, including clean-fuel investment, emissions monitoring and reductions, and asset retirement. Spending is expected to reach about $5.3 billion in 2022, with roughly 30% capital, and rise further in 2023 as low-carbon activities and emissions plans advance. Environmental liabilities are accrued when probable and estimable, including at current or former properties and multiparty remediation sites; no single site is expected to be material. Provisions were $146 million in 2021 versus $263 million in 2020, and year-end liabilities were $807 million versus $902 million.

nodes.title: MARKET RISKS
nodes.summary: The text reports worldwide average oil/NGL and natural-gas realizations for 2019–2021 and estimates that 2022 changes of $1 per barrel in oil or $0.10 per thousand cubic feet in gas would affect annual after-tax Upstream earnings by about $500 million or $155 million, respectively, excluding derivatives. Actual effects depend on grades, trading, taxes, contract lags, and volumes; Downstream and Chemical earnings depend mainly on margins. It discusses market volatility, financial strength, integrated segment sales at market prices, long-term supply-and-demand economics, investment reviews, and asset improvement or divestment. Risk management includes diversification, commodity derivatives and trading, counterparty controls, immaterial currency/interest-rate derivatives and interest exposure, liquidity and debt funding, possible joint-venture funding constraints, and limited, immaterial foreign-exchange hedging.

nodes.title: CRITICAL ACCOUNTING ESTIMATES
key_items: Energy Outlook and Cash Flow Assessment; Fair Value of Impaired Assets
Energy Outlook and Cash Flow Assessment
Asset Retirement Obligations; Suspended Exploratory Well Costs
Pension Benefits; Litigation and Tax Contingencies
nodes.summary: The section explains critical accounting estimates across the Corporation’s integrated energy businesses and the judgments required under GAAP. It covers reserve estimation, classifications, revisions and their use in unit-of-production depreciation; impairment indicators, planning assumptions, cash-flow and fair-value methods, other asset impairment tests, and impairment charges in 2019–2021 and potential future risks. It also discusses asset retirement obligations, suspended exploratory well costs, funded and unfunded pension accounting and assumptions, and recognition and disclosure of litigation and uncertain tax contingencies.

nodes.title: MANAGEMENT’S REPORT ON INTERNAL CONTROL OVER FINANCIAL REPORTING
key_items: Opinions on the Financial Statements and Internal Control over Financial Reporting; Basis for Opinions; Definition and Limitations of Internal Control over Financial Reporting
Opinions on the Financial Statements and Internal Control over Financial Reporting
Definition and Limitations of Internal Control over Financial Reporting
The Impact of Proved Oil and Natural Gas Reserves on Upstream Property, Plant and Equipment, Net
nodes.summary: Management reports that Exxon Mobil’s internal financial reporting controls were effective at December 31, 2021, based on the COSO 2013 framework, and identifies the responsible executives. PwC’s independent audit gives unqualified opinions on the 2021–2020 balance sheets, three years of financial statements, and 2021 internal controls; it describes management and auditor responsibilities, audit procedures, and control limitations. The report identifies reserve estimates’ effect on upstream property and equipment and depreciation as a critical audit matter, explaining its judgmental complexity and audit testing. PwC signed in Dallas on February 23, 2022, and notes it has served as auditor since 1934.

nodes.title: CONSOLIDATED STATEMENT OF INCOME
nodes.summary: Consolidated income statement for 2021, 2020, and 2019, in millions of dollars, presenting sales and other operating revenue, equity affiliate income, other income, and total revenues; operating and other costs and deductions; income or loss before taxes, tax expense or benefit, net income or loss including and attributable to noncontrolling interests, and net income or loss attributable to ExxonMobil. It also reports basic and diluted earnings or loss per common share and notes that the accompanying financial statement notes are integral to the statements.

nodes.title: CONSOLIDATED STATEMENT OF COMPREHENSIVE INCOME
nodes.summary: Consolidated statement of comprehensive income presents 2021, 2020, and 2019 figures in millions of dollars. It reports net income or loss including noncontrolling interests; other comprehensive income or loss, net of taxes, including foreign-exchange translation adjustments and related gains or losses in net income, and postretirement-benefit reserve adjustments and their amortization or settlement. It shows total other comprehensive income or loss, comprehensive income or loss, amounts attributable to noncontrolling interests, and amounts attributable to ExxonMobil. The accompanying notes are integral to the statements.

nodes.title: CONSOLIDATED BALANCE SHEET
nodes.summary: Presents ExxonMobil’s consolidated balance sheets for December 31, 2021 and 2020, detailing current and noncurrent assets, liabilities, commitments and contingencies, and equity, including year-over-year totals. Also reports consolidated cash flows for 2021, 2020, and 2019, covering operating adjustments and working-capital changes, investing activity, financing and debt transactions, dividends, exchange-rate effects, and beginning and ending cash. Notes to the financial statements are integral to both statements; a footnote clarifies debt maturity treatment.

nodes.title: CONSOLIDATED STATEMENT OF CHANGES IN EQUITY
nodes.summary: The consolidated statement of changes in equity reports ExxonMobil’s 2019–2021 movements in common stock, retained earnings, accumulated other comprehensive income, treasury stock, non-controlling interests, and total equity, including stock-award amortization, other changes, net income or loss, dividends, accounting changes, comprehensive income, acquisitions, and dispositions. It also presents issued, treasury, and outstanding share activity. Notes state that the financial statements and supporting material are management’s responsibility; describe the company’s oil, gas, product, specialty-product, and lower-emission businesses; explain that GAAP estimates affect reported amounts and disclosures and actual results may differ; and note certain prior-year reclassifications for 2021 comparability.

States that no separate Form 10-K summary is provided, then outlines the financial section and presents business and financial results, key definitions, forward-looking-statement risks, business strategy and operations, cash flow, liquidity, debt, obligations, capital and exploration spending, taxes, environmental costs and liabilities, market risks and hedging, and critical accounting estimates. It includes management’s internal-control report and the auditor’s opinions and critical audit matter; 2019–2021 income, comprehensive income, cash-flow, balance-sheet, and equity statements; and notes on the company, GAAP estimates, and prior-year reclassifications.

Covers ExxonMobil equity trading, dividends, share repurchases, and market-risk disclosures; financial statements, auditor reporting, and effective internal controls; proxy-incorporated governance, compensation, ownership, and equity-plan details; related-party transactions, director independence, auditor fees, and exhibit references. It provides no separate Form 10-K summary but outlines the financial section’s business and financial results, strategy, cash flow, liquidity, debt, spending, taxes, environmental and market risks, accounting estimates, controls and audit opinions, three-year financial statements, and notes.

summary: Summarizes oil and gas acreage rights, exploration and production terms, extensions, work commitments, and relinquishment rules across the United States, the Americas, Europe, Africa, Asia, Australia, and Papua New Guinea. Also covers ExxonMobil’s downstream refining and retail operations and chemical capacities; legal proceedings and mine-safety disclosures; executive officers; and subsequent Form 10-K matters, including trading, dividends, repurchases, financial statements, governance, controls, risks, and exhibits.

title: 1. Summary of Accounting Policies
key_items: Principles of Consolidation and Accounting for Investments; Revenue Recognition
Principles of Consolidation and Accounting for Investments
Income and Other Taxes; Derivative Instruments; Fair Value; Inventories
Energy Outlook and Cash Flow Assessment; Fair value of Impaired Assets; Other Impairments Related to Property, Plant and Equipment
Energy Outlook and Cash Flow Assessment
Other Impairments Related to Property, Plant and Equipment
summary: The accounting policies cover consolidation and equity investments, including control, equity method, impairment, and fair-value measurement; revenue recognition, customer contracts, taxes, and derivatives; fair-value input hierarchy; inventory costing; and property accounting under the successful-efforts method, depreciation, impairment indicators and valuation, planning assumptions, held-for-sale and unproved properties, gains, and capitalized interest. They also address environmental liabilities and foreign-currency functional currencies and transaction gains or losses.

title: 2. Restructuring Activities
summary: ExxonMobil reviewed global staffing in 2020 and implemented targeted workforce and contractor reductions, completed by the end of 2021, to improve efficiency and cut costs. The programs involved voluntary and involuntary separations. In 2021, it recorded $58 million in pre-tax separation costs for Singapore and Europe, in selling, general and administrative expenses within Corporate and Financing; no further charges are expected. The table reports program reserves and charges, excluding reductions tied to portfolio changes or other projects: the 2020 ending balance of $403 million became the 2021 opening balance; 2021 additions were $58 million, payments $384 million, and the ending liability $77 million. Recorded in accounts payable and accrued liabilities, this balance will be paid over the next few years, mainly monthly.

title: 3. Miscellaneous Financial Information
summary: Reports 2019–2021 R&D expenses, foreign-exchange transaction losses, and LIFO-related inventory gains; compares estimated replacement cost with LIFO carrying value and lists year-end inventories by category for 2020 and 2021. Describes 2020 goodwill impairment charges and their valuation basis and income-statement classification. Presents 2019–2021 accumulated other comprehensive income movements for foreign-exchange translation and postretirement benefits, amounts reclassified to income, and related income-tax expense or credits, including net-investment-hedge effects.

title: Cash Flows and Working Capital
summary: Explains cash-equivalent classification and cash-flow statement items, including 2021 UK North Sea and Santoprene asset sales, 2019 Norway asset sales, and 2020 impairment effects on depreciation and deferred taxes. Reports 2019–2021 income taxes and cash interest paid, including capitalized interest. Provides 2020–2021 receivables, notes and loans payable, and accounts payable and accrued liability balances. Notes $10.7 billion in unused committed short-term credit lines at year-end 2021 and short-term borrowing rates of 0.2% in both years.

title: 7. Equity Company Information
summary: Note 7 describes equity companies’ industries and regions, ExxonMobil sales share (10%, 11%, and 13% in 2021–2019), investment structures, accounting for carrying-value differences, and upstream impairments. It summarizes 2021, 2020, and 2019 equity-company financial results and assets, and lists significant 2021 ventures by upstream, downstream, and chemical sector with ownership percentages. Note 8 reports 2021 and 2020 equity-method investments and advances, fair-value and other investments, long-term receivables, and total balances.

title: 9. Property, Plant and Equipment and Asset Retirement Obligations
summary: The note reports PPE cost and net book values by business segment for 2021 and 2020, impairment assessments and charges for 2019–2021, and accumulated depreciation and depletion. It explains how asset retirement obligations (AROs) are measured, capitalized, depreciated, and accreted, and why obligations for certain downstream and chemical sites cannot yet be measured. It also provides the 2019–2021 ARO liability rollforward, long-term ARO balances at year-end 2021 and 2020, and estimated cash payments for 2022 and 2023.

title: 10. Accounting for Suspended Exploratory Well Costs
summary: The note explains when exploratory well costs remain capitalized: sufficient reserves must support completion, with progress assessing reserves and project viability. It presents 2019–2021 changes in suspended-cost balances, aging by capitalization period, and project counts by cost age. Of 30 projects with costs capitalized over one year in 2021, 13 had recent or planned activity; the other 17, totaling $2.874 billion, are detailed by country and project, with balances, drilling/acquisition years, and development, infrastructure, commercialization, or government-discussion status.

title: 11. Leases
summary: Notes describe ExxonMobil’s leasing practices: most assets are purchased; leases are mainly for drilling equipment, vessels, buildings, railcars and other equipment. They explain lease-term and discount-rate assumptions, operating versus finance classification, excluded service costs, and immaterial variable payments, guarantees, restrictions, related-party transactions and lessor activity. Tables report 2019–2021 lease costs, balance-sheet right-of-use assets and liabilities, terms and rates, 2021 payment maturities, uncommenced commitments and cash-flow/noncash information; finance leases include vessels and a hydrogen purchase agreement. Earnings-per-share data for 2019–2021 include net income/loss, weighted-average shares, earnings per share, and dividends; diluted and basic earnings per share are equal.

title: 13. Financial Instruments and Derivatives
summary: The notes disclose 2021 and 2020 fair values and hierarchy levels for financial assets and liabilities, including derivatives, equity-company balances, debt and other obligations, with balance-sheet classifications and valuation methods for Level 3 items. They report collateral held under master netting arrangements that was not offset. The Corporation describes derivative risk management, trading and accounting practices, counterparty controls, and immaterial currency and interest-rate derivatives. Net commodity derivative positions for crude oil, petroleum products and natural gas, and realized and unrealized derivative gains or losses by income-statement line for 2019–2021, are also provided.

title: 14. Long-Term Debt
summary: The note details Exxon Mobil’s 2021 long-term debt: $43.428 billion excluding $2.392 billion due within one year, the extinguishment of 2.397% notes due 2022, maturities for 2023–2026, and $0.6 billion of unused credit lines. It explains the accounting for foreign-currency debt hedges and the perfectly effective $5.1 billion Euro-debt net investment hedge. A table compares 2021 and 2020 debt by notes, bonds, currency, leases, and issuance costs, with average rates and premium footnotes.

title: Incentive Program and Restricted Stock Awards
summary: Describes the 2003 Incentive Program’s eligible awards, grant and forfeiture rules, limits, duration, and 66 million shares available at year-end 2021. Summarizes restricted stock and unit grants, vesting schedules, restrictions, accounting, and 2021 activity and grant-date values. Reports unrecognized compensation cost and recognition period, compensation expense and tax benefits for 2019–2021, vested award values, and cash settlements.

title: 16. Litigation and Other Contingencies
summary: Note 16 describes litigation and contingency accounting and disclosure policies, guarantees and contingent obligations, long-term commitments, and ongoing Venezuelan and Nigerian claims, which are not expected to materially affect ExxonMobil. Note 17 details pension and postretirement benefit assumptions, obligations, assets, costs, funded status and balance-sheet/AOCI effects; funding and investment strategies; 2020–2021 asset fair values by category and hierarchy; underfunded plans; and expected 2022 contributions and future benefit payments.

title: 18. Disclosures about Segments and Related Information
summary: The disclosure defines Upstream, Downstream, and Chemical as reportable operating segments based on their activities, regular review by the chief operating decision maker, and availability of separate financial data. It explains estimated-market-price transfers and Corporate and Financing interest revenue and expense, including non-debt interest expense for 2019–2021. Segment tables present earnings, equity-company earnings, revenues, intersegment revenue, depreciation, interest, taxes, capital additions, equity investments, and assets for 2019–2021. Geographic revenue totals are reported by U.S. and non-U.S. operations, with major non-U.S. sources listed; attribution is by primary country of operations, excluding certain revenues that cannot practicably be assigned.

title: Long-lived assets
summary: Reports long-lived assets by U.S. and non-U.S. regions for 2019–2021, including significant non-U.S. asset locations. Presents income tax expense or benefit and other taxes and duties by U.S. and non-U.S. sources for those years, with notes on deferred-tax benefits from tax-law changes and 2020 impairments. Reconciles tax expense to the 21% theoretical U.S. rate and gives effective tax rates, with explanations of notable 2020 and 2019 adjustments. Details deferred-tax liabilities, assets, valuation allowances, and 2021 allowance changes.

title: Balance sheet classification
summary: The text presents 2021 and 2020 balance-sheet figures for other assets, deferred income tax liabilities, and net deferred tax liabilities. It explains that foreign subsidiary earnings are indefinitely reinvested, so potential withholding and state taxes are not accrued; estimating the related unrecognized liability is impracticable, though it is not expected to be material. It also describes how uncertain tax positions are recognized and measured, defines unrecognized tax benefits, and introduces a table summarizing their movement.

title: Gross unrecognized tax benefits
summary: The table reports gross unrecognized tax benefits for 2019–2021, including opening and closing balances and changes from current- and prior-year tax positions, statute expirations, settlements, and other effects. Most balances relate to positions that would lower the effective tax rate if favorably resolved; changes did not materially affect net income, and resolution may take years. The text describes ongoing U.S. federal tax disputes dating to 2006, litigation and appeals over 2006–2009 positions, and penalties the Corporation does not expect to apply. An unfavorable resolution would not materially harm operations or financial condition. Benefits could rise up to 10% or fall up to 70% in the next 12 months, mainly due to possible litigation resolution; a following table summarizes examination periods by major jurisdiction.

title: Country of Operation
summary: Lists the Corporation’s operating countries and their open tax years: Abu Dhabi (2020–2021), Angola (2018–2021), Australia (2010–2021), Belgium (2017–2021), Canada (2001–2021), Equatorial Guinea (2007–2021), Indonesia (2008–2021), Iraq (2016–2021), Malaysia (2017–2021), Nigeria (2006–2021), Papua New Guinea (2008–2021), Russia (2019–2021), United Kingdom (2015–2021), and United States (2006–2021). Tax-related interest is classified as interest expense or income, and penalties as operating expense. Net interest expense on income tax reserves was $0 million in 2021 and 2019 and a $6 million credit in 2020; interest payable was $61 million at December 31, 2021 and 2020.

title: SUPPLEMENTAL INFORMATION ON OIL AND GAS EXPLORATION AND PRODUCTION ACTIVITIES (unaudited)
summary: Unaudited supplemental oil and gas exploration and production information presents regional results of operations for the United States, Canada/Other Americas, Australia/Oceania, Europe, Africa, Asia, and total, for 2021, 2020, and 2019. Tables distinguish consolidated subsidiaries from equity companies and report third-party sales, transfers, production and exploration costs, depreciation and depletion, non-income taxes, related income taxes, producing-activity results, and total results. The figures exclude specified other Upstream activities, whose combined amounts were losses of $1.380 billion in 2021 and earnings of $274 million in 2020 and $3.502 billion in 2019; oil sands mining is included under SEC and FASB rules.

title: Oil and Gas Exploration and Production Costs
summary: The text explains that consolidated subsidiaries’ net capitalized oil and gas costs were $12.005 billion lower in 2021 and $13.206 billion lower in 2020 than Upstream property, plant and equipment investments because certain transportation, research and LNG assets are excluded; oil sands and shale mining assets are included under accounting rules. It then presents 2021 and 2020 capitalized-cost data for consolidated subsidiaries and equity companies by region, covering proved and unproved acreage, producing and construction assets, total and accumulated depreciation/depletion, and net capitalized costs.

title: Oil and Gas Exploration and Production Costs (continued)
summary: Reports 2019–2021 oil and gas exploration, acquisition, and development costs by region and consolidated versus equity companies, explaining annual changes. Defines proved, developed, and undeveloped reserves; SEC pricing and estimation rules; revision factors; ownership and production-sharing treatment; and production-volume distinctions. Presents regional reserve balances and movements for liquids, natural gas, and oil-equivalent products, including developed/undeveloped and consolidated/equity totals. Highlights 2021 reserve increases from bitumen revisions and discoveries, production, and 2020 price- and spending-related downward revisions.

title: Standardized Measure of Discounted Future Cash Flows
key_items: Standardized Measure of Discounted Future Cash Flows
summary: Explains the FASB-prescribed standardized measure: estimated future net cash flows from proved reserves use first-day-of-month average prices, year-end costs, legislated tax rates, and a 10% discount rate, including future dismantlement, abandonment, and rehabilitation costs. The Corporation cautions that the measure is not a reliable estimate of expected cash flows or reserve value, since prescribed point-in-time prices can cause year-to-year variability. Tables report future inflows, production and development costs, taxes, net cash flows, discount effects, and discounted totals as of December 31, 2019, for consolidated subsidiaries and equity companies across geographic regions and in total. A footnote notes that Canada/Other Americas includes $1.064 billion attributable to noncontrolling interests in consolidated subsidiaries.

title: Standardized Measure of Discounted Future Cash Flows (continued)
summary: Presents standardized discounted future cash flow measures for proved oil and gas reserves at December 31, 2020 and 2021, by consolidated subsidiaries and equity companies across the United States, Canada/Other Americas, Europe, Africa, Australia/Oceania, and Asia. Components include projected sales, production and development costs, income taxes, net cash flows, and the 10% discount effect; totals are reported, with a note on noncontrolling interests. Also reconciles 2019 and 2020 changes in discounted future net cash flows for consolidated subsidiaries, equity-method investees, and combined interests, showing reserve additions, production, development spending, price/cost changes, estimate revisions, discount accretion, taxes, and year-end balances.

title: Consolidated and Equity Interests
summary: The text presents annual reconciliations of the standardized measure of discounted future net cash flows for proved oil and gas reserves in 2019, 2020, and 2021. For each year, it reports opening and closing values and changes from reserve additions, production net of lifting costs, development spending, price and cost changes, estimate revisions, discount accretion, and income taxes. Amounts are shown in millions of dollars for consolidated subsidiaries, equity-method investees, and their combined total.

title: INDEX TO EXHIBITS

nodes.title: INDEX TO EXHIBITS (intro)
nodes.summary: The exhibit index lists ExxonMobil’s incorporation and capital-stock documents; bylaws; incentive, restricted-stock, bonus, savings, pension, additional-payment, life-insurance, and director compensation plans and instruments; its Code of Ethics; subsidiary list; PwC consent; officer certifications under Exchange Act Rule 13a-14(a) and Sarbanes-Oxley Section 906; Inline XBRL data and cover-page files. It notes designated compensatory arrangements and states that long-term debt instruments are omitted but will be furnished to the SEC upon request. The report concludes with an authorized signature statement under the Exchange Act.

POWER OF ATTORNEY
nodes.summary: Exxon Mobil Chairman Darren W. Woods signed the document on February 23, 2022. It grants Jeremy R. Osterstock, Antony E. Peters, and David R. Woodcock authority to sign and file amendments to the Form 10-K and related materials with the SEC. The report is signed under the Securities Exchange Act of 1934 by Woods as Chairman and Principal Executive Officer, directors Michael J. Angelakis, Susan K. Avery, Angela F. Braly, Ursula M. Burns, Kenneth C. Frazier, Gregory J. Goff, Kaisa H. Hietala, Joseph L. Hooley, Steven A. Kandarian, Alexander A. Karsner, and Jeffrey W. Ubben, and financial officers Kathryn A. Mikells and Len M. Fox. Exhibit 10(iii)(a.3) follows.

nodes.title: Exxon Mobil Corporation 2021 Extended Provisions for Restricted Stock Unit Agreements Settled in Stock
nodes.summary: ExxonMobil’s 2021 stock-settled restricted stock unit agreement for a non-employee director sets an acceptance deadline of March 1, 2022, and provides that each unit represents one future common share. Units are nontransferable and generally vest in 50% installments on November 23, 2026 and 2031, with restrictions ending at death. It defines pre-credit and post-credit forfeiture for early termination, detrimental activity, attempted transfers, legal or policy requirements, and clawbacks; permits tax withholding; and provides for share settlement, dividend equivalents, and capitalization adjustments. Units confer no shareholder status and remain subject to legal and listing limits. The agreement also covers access to the Program, communications, personal-data processing and rights, no employment or future-award entitlement, New York law and Texas venue, and the entire-agreement provision.

nodes.title: EXHIBIT 10(iii)(f.3)
nodes.summary: Stephen A. Littleton’s letter informs the recipient of a January 3, 2022 grant of 2,500 Exxon Mobil restricted shares under the 2004 Non-Employee Director Restricted Stock Plan and refers them to the Plan for full terms. Shares are held in book-entry form; the recipient may vote and receive cash dividends but cannot transfer or encumber them during the restricted period. Restrictions end upon qualifying Board departure after retirement age, good-standing departure before that age, or death, when shares are delivered free of restrictions. Acceptance confirms agreement to the terms and forfeiture conditions. The recipient may designate a beneficiary and is advised of enclosed tax and Securities Act information, with contact details provided for questions and beneficiary forms.
